source_title: Best of Business Standard Opinion: Resilience comes from widening the base - Business Standard
source_excerpt: You can’t build resilience by putting everything behind one answer. A household that leans too heavily on gold-backed borrowing becomes vulnerable to asset prices. An investor who treats an entire sector as one trade can miss differences between firms. A country that relies on a single policy tool to manage external stress discovers its limits. Agriculture becomes more fragile when crop diversity narrows. Even knowledge systems are stronger when authority is distributed rather than concentrated. “Glitter of gold loans”, our first editorial today, looks at the rapid growth of household borrowing against gold. Gold is convenient collateral and gives lenders security, which explains why these loans are popular. But the editorial warns that the pace of expansion deserves scrutiny. When household borrowing rises alongside high gold prices, apparent comfort can conceal underlying stress. A strong collateral asset does not eliminate repayment risk, and excessive dependence on gold-backed credit can become a vulnerability if household finances weaken or asset prices reverse. The second editorial, “Value buying”, looks at Indian IT sector. Artificial intelligence is reshaping this sector, changing client spending and causing company strategies to diverge. That makes blanket sector calls less useful. Investors need to look more closely at productivity, adaptability, valuations, client exposure and each company’s ability to navigate technological change. Indian IT is no longer one homogeneous bet; resilience in investing comes from distinguishing between firms rather than treating the sector as a single trade. In “Ten rules for external sector stress”, Ajay Shah, K P Krishnan and G Padmanabhan make the diversification argument more directly. External shocks cannot be managed through one instrument, whether that is defending the rupee, using reserves or tightening monetary policy. Exchange-rate flexibility, fiscal discipline, banking resilience, capital flows, reserves and institutional credibility all have a role. The lesson from past episodes of stress is to maintain several lines of defence rather than place excessive faith in any one of them. Surinder Sud’s column, “The neglected species of pulses”, brings the theme to agriculture. India’s focus on a relatively small group of major pulses has left many traditional varieties underused. Yet these crops can offer nutritional benefits, suit different agroclimatic conditions and improve resilience to climate stress. A more diverse crop basket can strengthen both food security and farm resilience. “Wikipedia’s origin story, warts and all”, Jennifer Szalai’s review of Richard Cooke’s The Last Best Place on the Internet, turns to knowledge. Wikipedia grew by distributing the creation and correction of information across a vast community rather than concentrating authority among a small editorial elite. That openness created governance problems of its own, but it also made the platform unusually adaptive. Resilience, as we see across all these pieces, comes from widening the base — spreading risk and avoiding dependence on a single answer.
